docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
minevent is a Python library that provides a minimal event system for Machine Learning. It allows you to customize code by adding pieces of code that are executed when an event is fired. minevent is organized around three main concepts:

  • event which defines the thing that should happen.
  • event handler which is any callable to execute when the event happens
  • event manager which is responsible to manage the events and event handlers.

The goal of this documentation is to explain how the event system works and how to use it. The library provides some implemented modules, but it is possible to extend it. It is possible to use all the components or just a subset based on the need. For example, a handler is a plain callable, so it can be tested without the event manager.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
minevent provides a minimal event system to customize a piece of code without changing its implementation. Below is an example on how to use minevent library.

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def say_something(manager: EventManager) -> None:
...     print("Hello, I am Bob!")
...     manager.trigger_event("after")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> say_something(manager)
Hello, I am Bob!
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("after", hello_handler)
>>> say_something(manager)
Hello, I am Bob!
Hello!

It allows you to customize the function say_something without changing its implementation. Please read the quickstart page to learn more about the library.

docs.title: API stability
docs.text: While minevent is in development stage, no API is guaranteed to be stable from one release to the next. In fact, it is very likely that the API will change multiple times before a stable 1.0.0 release. In practice, this means that upgrading minevent to a new version will possibly break any code that was using the old version of minevent.

docs.title: Architecture and Design Principles
docs.text: This document describes the architecture and design principles of minevent.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
These properties hold for every release and each one is covered by tests.

# Property Statement Enforced by P1 Small surface Events are strings, handlers are plain callables, the manager connects them. Six exported names and __version__ (EventManager, Subscription, Context, Condition, PeriodicCondition, AfterNCondition). EventManager has 8 public members (events, get_subscriptions, add_event_handler, on, trigger_event, atrigger_event, clear_event, reset) and __len__, __contains__. test_init.py P2 Cheap import import minevent is cheap and has no side effect: standard library only, and not logging, inspect, asyncio or importlib.metadata, and it creates no typing object (NamedTuple, Protocol, TypeVar): the annotations are strings and typing is read under TYPE_CHECKING only (inspect is imported when the first handler is registered, the version on the first access of __version__). It starts no thread, reads no file, emits no warning and writes no log. test_import.py (modules and typing objects) P3 Events are strings An event name is a case-sensitive str; any other type raises TypeError. The empty string is valid. Reading the manager never creates an event. test_manager.py P4 Validated at the door A wrong type raises TypeError in the call that receives it, with a message that names the argument and the value: the event, the handler (must be callable) and the condition (None or callable) of add_event_handler and on. An invalid registration leaves the manager unchanged. add_event_handler, on, test_manager.py P5 Registration identity add_event_handler returns a new Subscription every time; the same callable can be registered several times. remove() removes that registration only, once: True the first time, then False. active is True from the registration until the registration is removed, by whatever means. Subscription, test_manager.py P6 Registration order The handlers of an event run in the order they were registered, one after the other, in the calling thread. the ordered dict, test_manager.py P7 Snapshot dispatch trigger_event runs the registrations that exist when it starts. A registration added by a running handler takes effect at the next trigger. A registration removed before its turn (by remove(), clear_event, reset or a once claim) does not run: a removed registration never starts. Subscription._call, test_manager.py P8 Fail-fast with context An exception of a handler propagates unchanged (same object, same type); the remaining handlers are skipped. It carries a note with the event and the name of the handler (the function under a functools.partial), once per distinct pair. No message and no repr of the package runs the repr of user data: they name the function, never its arguments. _describe, _add_error_note, test_manager.py P9 once is at-most-once A once registration is removed by an atomic claim just before its handler runs, so it runs at most once whatever the number of threads. A false condition does not consume it (the condition is evaluated first); a handler that raises does consume it. Subscription._call, test_manager_once.py, test_manager_threads.py P10 Synchronous by default trigger_event never awaits; a handler that returns an awaitable raises TypeError and the coroutine is closed. atrigger_event awaits the handlers one after the other; synchronous handlers run inline and block the loop. An object with async def __call__ is a coroutine handler like a coroutine function. _check_not_awaitable, test_manager_async.py P11 Thread-safe registry The registry is protected by a reentrant lock. Handlers, conditions and the repr of user objects run outside the lock, so a handler can use the manager. EventManager._lock, test_manager_threads.py P12 No hidden state No global manager, no discovery, no side effect of a read. Zero runtime dependencies; the import is cheap (P2). A manager cannot be copied or pickled (copy.copy, copy.deepcopy and pickle raise the same TypeError). __reduce__, test_manager.py P13 Payload is data trigger_event(event, context=None, /) copies the mapping context (a dict, for example), or reuses a Context as is, into one read-only Context per trigger, shared by the handlers. A handler with a parameter is called as handler(context), a handler without parameter as handler(); the check counts parameters once, at registration, and never matches keys. Any str key is allowed, it does not need to be a valid identifier. The handler decides what a missing key means (context[key] or context.get(key, default)). Arguments that do not come from the payload are bound with functools.partial: the manager has no second mechanism. trigger_event, test_manager.py P14 Options are per registration once and condition are keyword-only arguments of add_event_handler and on, with the same names, defaults and meaning in both. A condition is a function that returns a boolean, called once per trigger, before the handler: as condition(context) if it has a parameter, and as condition() otherwise (the rule of the handlers). The built-in conditions keep per-instance state and both have reset(). signatures, test_manager.py, test_conditions.py P15 Typed Fully typed, py.typed, ty check clean, the values of a Context are typed object. ty check in CI P16 Fast and linear A trigger of one handler costs about 0.33 µs with no data (0.7 µs with a small dict, which is copied into a Context), each extra handler about 0.1 µs, a registration plus its removal about 0.65 µs (Python 3.14, laptop). Registering k handlers and removing them in any order costs O(k) in total. Benchmarks guard it. tests/benchmarks/ P17 A manager is a service bool(manager) is always True, empty or not, so manager or default means "is there a manager". len(manager) is the number of registrations. __bool__, test_manager.py P18 One way to do each thing One way to register (add_event_handler, with on as its decorator form), one way to bind arguments (functools.partial), one way to run a handler once (once=True, whatever the condition), one way to extend (write a callable). No handler base class. the signatures P19 Debuggable without a logger repr(subscription) names the event and the handler function (Subscription(event='epoch_end', handler='log_epoch')), repr(manager) counts the registrations per event. The library logs nothing: get_subscriptions(event) is the way to look. __repr__, test_manager.py

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
minevent is designed as a minimal event system with three core components:

  1. Events - String identifiers representing things that happen
  2. Event Handlers - Any callable that executes when events occur
  3. Event Manager - Coordinator that manages handlers and triggers events

docs.title: 1. Simplicity First
docs.text:
minevent prioritizes simplicity over features:

  • Minimal API surface area
  • Easy to understand and use
  • No complex configuration required
  • Clear separation of concerns

Example: Events are simply strings, not complex objects.

# Simple and clear
manager.trigger_event("training_complete")

# Not: complex event objects
# manager.trigger_event(Event(name="training_complete", priority=1, ...))

docs.title: 2. Synchronous by Design
docs.text:
trigger_event is synchronous:

  • Handlers execute in the order they were registered
  • Easy to reason about execution flow
  • Simpler debugging and testing
  • Coroutine handlers are opt-in with atrigger_event
  • The registry is protected by a lock, but the library starts no thread

Rationale: ML workflows are often sequential and benefit from deterministic execution order.

docs.title: 3. Explicit Over Implicit
docs.text:
All actions are explicit:

  • Must explicitly register handlers
  • Must explicitly trigger events
  • Must explicitly pass arguments to handlers

Example:

# Explicit registration
manager.add_event_handler("event", handler)

# Explicit triggering
manager.trigger_event("event")

# Not: implicit auto-registration or magic discovery

docs.title: 4. Extensibility Through Composition
docs.text:
Extend functionality by composing callables:

  • A handler is any callable: a function, a method, a callable object or a functools.partial
  • The options of a registration (once, condition) are arguments of add_event_handler
  • No base class and no inheritance

Example:

# Compose a handler with a condition, and bind an argument with functools.partial
manager.add_event_handler(
    "epoch_end",
    functools.partial(my_function, verbose=True),
    condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=5),
)


# Custom conditions: any function that returns a bool, with or without the context
class MyCondition:
    def __call__(self) -> bool:
        return custom_logic()

docs.title: 5. Zero Magic
docs.text:
No hidden behavior or surprising actions:

  • No global state
  • No automatic discovery
  • No metaclasses and no discovery; the only introspection is the count of the parameters of a handler at registration (does it need the context?) and the check of an awaitable result
  • What you write is what happens

docs.title: Event
docs.text:
Design: Events are represented as case-sensitive strings.

Rationale:

  • Simple and universal
  • Easy to type and understand
  • No serialization issues
  • Language-agnostic concept

Best Practices:

  • Use descriptive names
  • Follow consistent naming convention
  • Use a namespace such as training.batch.end for complex systems (names are plain strings, so there is no hierarchy)

docs.title: Event Handler
docs.text:
Design: A handler is any callable. The manager calls it as handler(context) if it has a parameter that accepts a positional argument, and as handler() otherwise.

Rationale:

  • A callable already is the extension point: there is no base class to learn or to import
  • Arguments that do not come from the payload are bound with functools.partial, so there is one way to bind them, and the parameter count sees the signature of the partial (the arguments that it binds are not counted)
  • A handler that returns an awaitable (a coroutine function, or an object with async def __call__) is awaited by atrigger_event; trigger_event raises a TypeError
  • A Subscription identifies a registration, so the same callable can be registered several times

docs.title: Event Manager
docs.text:
Design: Central coordinator using a dictionary to map events to ordered sets of subscriptions.

Internal Structure:

{
    "event1": {subscription1: None, subscription2: None, subscription3: None},
    "event2": {subscription4: None, subscription5: None},
    # ...
}

Rationale:

  • Simple dictionary lookup for handlers
  • Preserves registration order
  • Easy to implement and understand

Key Operations:

  • O(1) handler registration
  • O(n) event triggering (n = number of handlers)
  • O(1) removal of a registration

docs.title: Registration Options
docs.text:
Design: The options of a registration are the keyword-only arguments of add_event_handler (on is its decorator form, with the same options). The Subscription stores them.

Architecture:

add_event_handler(event, handler, *, once=False, condition=None)
    └── Subscription (event, handler, once, condition)

Execution Flow:

trigger_event()
    ├── Get the subscriptions of the event
    └── For each subscription:
        ├── If it has a condition: evaluate it, and skip the handler if it is False
        ├── If it is a once registration: remove it, and skip it if it was already removed
        └── Execute handler(context), or handler() if it has no parameter

Rationale:

  • Separates "what" (handler) from "when" (condition) and from "how" (options)
  • Conditions are reusable across handlers
  • Conditions can maintain state between evaluations

docs.title: Registration Flow
docs.text:
1. User registers a callable
   subscription = manager.add_event_handler("event", handler, once=..., condition=...)

2. Manager validates the arguments
   a TypeError names the event, the handler or the condition that is wrong

3. Manager stores the registration
   a Subscription is added to the ordered set of the event and returned

docs.title: Triggering Flow
docs.text:
1. User triggers event
   manager.trigger_event("event", {"key": value})

2. Manager gets the registrations
   subscriptions = a snapshot of the ordered set of the event
   context = Context(payload)   # one read-only context, shared by the handlers

3. Manager executes each handler
   for subscription in subscriptions:
       result = subscription._call(context)   # condition, once claim, handler(context) or handler()
       # an awaitable result raises a TypeError (trigger_event) or is awaited (atrigger_event)
       # an exception gets a note (event, handler function) and propagates

docs.title: Handler Execution
docs.text:
Without condition:
    handler(context)      # or handler() if it has no parameter

With a condition:
    if condition():
        handler(context)

The context is read-only: a handler cannot change what the next handler sees.
Arguments bound with functools.partial are part of `handler`, not of the payload.

docs.title: Custom Handlers
docs.text:
Write a callable. A class with a __call__ method is a handler with its own state:

class MyHandler:
    def __call__(self, context: Context) -> None:
        # Custom logic; context holds the data given to trigger_event
        pass


class MyAsyncHandler:
    async def __call__(self, context: Context) -> None:
        # Awaited by atrigger_event
        pass

Use Cases:

  • Handlers with complex state
  • Handlers that modify themselves
  • Handlers with special lifecycle

docs.title: Custom Conditions
docs.text:
A condition is any function that returns a boolean (a Condition): Callable[[], bool], or Callable[[Context], bool] to decide from the payload of the trigger. Implement __call__ in a class when the condition has a state:

class MyCondition:
    def __call__(self) -> bool:
        # Custom logic
        return some_condition

To combine conditions, write a function: lambda: a() and b() skips b when a is False, and lambda: all([a(), b()]) evaluates both.

Use Cases:

  • Time-based conditions
  • State-based conditions
  • Metric-threshold conditions
  • Complex multi-condition logic

docs.title: Not guaranteed
docs.text:
These behaviors are documented limits, not defects:

  • A removal in another thread. P7 is exact in the thread that triggers: a handler that removes a later registration of the same trigger prevents it. Another thread that calls remove() while a trigger is between the check and the call of that handler cannot prevent that one start. After a trigger returns, a removed registration has not run.
  • Recursion. A handler that triggers its own event recurses until RecursionError.
  • Blocking. A synchronous handler in atrigger_event blocks the event loop.
  • A handler that returns a generator (a def with yield) does nothing: the generator is never iterated. Only awaitables are detected (P10).
  • Prompt reclamation. A manager that holds a registration is in a reference cycle (manager, dict, Subscription, manager): del manager does not free it until the garbage collector runs. Call reset() to release the handlers at a known point.
  • A callable whose signature cannot be inspected is called as handler(context). If it takes no argument, the call raises a TypeError with the note of the event and the handler: wrap it in a function without parameter.
  • A mutable value of the payload. The Context is read-only, but its values are not copied: a handler that mutates a list is seen by the next handlers.

docs.title: Thread Safety
docs.text:
Status: EventManager protects its registry with a reentrant lock. Registering, removing and inspecting handlers, and triggering events, can be done from several threads.

Guarantees:

  • trigger_event runs the handlers of a snapshot taken under the lock; the handlers run outside the lock, in the calling thread, so a handler can use the manager.
  • Handlers added or removed during a trigger take effect on the next trigger.

Not guaranteed:

  • Handlers triggered from several threads run concurrently. A handler that shares state must protect it.
  • The state of a condition (for example the counter of PeriodicCondition) is not protected, so a stateful condition should be triggered from one thread.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
minevent stays minimal. These features are not provided and are not planned:

  • Event objects with metadata or priorities: events are plain strings, and data is given as a dict (or a Context) to trigger_event.
  • Handler ordering other than the registration order.
  • Weak references or sender/receiver filtering.
  • Collecting handler errors: handlers run fail-fast, and an exception stops the dispatch. To run every handler and report all the failures, wrap the handler in a try/except (an ExceptionGroup option such as on_error="collect" was considered and declined to keep trigger_event minimal).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: This page shows how to use minevent in practical situations. Every example runs as written: the quickstart explains the API step by step, and the user guide lists the recommendations.

docs.title: Add logging to a training loop
docs.text:
The training loop triggers events and knows nothing about the handlers. The caller decides what happens, so logging, checkpointing or monitoring is added without changing the loop:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def train(manager: EventManager, epochs: int) -> None:
...     manager.trigger_event("training_start")
...     for epoch in range(epochs):
...         loss = 1.0 / (epoch + 1)
...         manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch, "loss": loss})
...     manager.trigger_event("training_end")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> train(manager, epochs=2)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("training_start", lambda: print("Training started"))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end", lambda context: print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}: loss={context['loss']}")
... )
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("training_end", lambda: print("Training ended"))
>>> train(manager, epochs=2)
Training started
epoch 0: loss=1.0
epoch 1: loss=0.5
Training ended

The first call of train prints nothing because no handler is registered.

docs.title: Run a handler every N epochs
docs.text:
Give the registration a condition. PeriodicCondition(freq=3) is True on the first call and then every three calls; skip_first=True skips the first call:

>>> from minevent import EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end",
...     lambda context: print(f"checkpoint at epoch {context['epoch']}"),
...     condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=3, skip_first=True),
... )
>>> for epoch in range(7):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch})
checkpoint at epoch 3
checkpoint at epoch 6

AfterNCondition(n) is False for the first n calls, which is useful for a warm-up:

>>> from minevent import AfterNCondition, EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end",
...     lambda context: print(f"validate at epoch {context['epoch']}"),
...     condition=AfterNCondition(2),
... )
>>> for epoch in range(4):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch})
validate at epoch 2
validate at epoch 3

docs.title: Write a custom condition
docs.text:
A condition is any function that returns a boolean, without parameter or with the Context of the trigger (see the next example). A class with __call__ is useful when the condition has a state or reads another object:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> class Flag:
...     def __init__(self) -> None:
...         self.enabled = False
...
...     def __call__(self) -> bool:
...         return self.enabled
>>> verbose = Flag()
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", lambda: print("batch done"), condition=verbose)
>>> manager.trigger_event("batch_end")
>>> verbose.enabled = True
>>> manager.trigger_event("batch_end")
batch done

To combine conditions, write a function, for example condition=lambda: a() and b().

docs.title: Decide from the payload
docs.text:
A condition that has a parameter is called with the same read-only Context as the handlers, so it can depend on the payload of the trigger. A condition without parameter is called without argument. A handler and its condition can read different keys:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def is_improving(context: Context) -> bool:
...     return context.get("loss", 1.0) < 0.5
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end",
...     lambda context: print(f"save the model of epoch {context['epoch']}"),
...     condition=is_improving,
... )
>>> for epoch, loss in enumerate([0.9, 0.4, 0.6, 0.3]):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch, "loss": loss})
save the model of epoch 1
save the model of epoch 3

The built-in conditions (PeriodicCondition, AfterNCondition) take no parameter. To combine one with a condition on the payload, write a function that calls it: condition=lambda context: periodic() and is_improving(context).

docs.title: Keep a state in a handler
docs.text:
A class with a __call__(self, context) method is a handler with its own state. This one collects the losses and is read after the training:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> class LossHistory:
...     def __init__(self) -> None:
...         self.losses = []
...
...     def __call__(self, context: Context) -> None:
...         self.losses.append(context["loss"])
>>> history = LossHistory()
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", history)
>>> for epoch, loss in enumerate([0.9, 0.6, 0.4]):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch, "loss": loss})
>>> history.losses
[0.9, 0.6, 0.4]

The handler ignores the keys that it does not read, here epoch.

docs.title: Share an event between handlers with different needs
docs.text:
Each handler receives the same read-only Context and reads the keys that it needs. A handler decides what to do with a missing key: context["lr"] raises a KeyError, and context.get("lr", 0.1) returns a default:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def log_loss(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"loss {context['loss']}")
>>> def log_epoch(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}, lr {context.get('lr', 0.1)}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", log_loss)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", log_epoch)
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 3, "loss": 0.5})
loss 0.5
epoch 3, lr 0.1

docs.title: Register with a decorator
docs.text:
on registers a function and returns it unchanged, so the function can still be called directly. It takes the same options as add_event_handler:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> @manager.on("epoch_end", condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=2))
... def log_epoch(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}")
>>> for epoch in range(3):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch})
epoch 0
epoch 2
>>> log_epoch(Context({"epoch": 10}))
epoch 10

docs.title: Pass a dict or a Context
docs.text:
trigger_event takes the data of the trigger as a dict, or as a Context. Both give the handlers the same read-only Context. A dict is copied and validated at each trigger, while a Context is validated once, when it is built, and is passed as is, so build it once to reuse it:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end", lambda context: print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}, loss {context['loss']}")
... )
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 3, "loss": 0.5})
epoch 3, loss 0.5
>>> context = Context({"epoch": 4, "loss": 0.4})
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", context)
epoch 4, loss 0.4
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", context)
epoch 4, loss 0.4

docs.title: Bind fixed arguments
docs.text:
Use functools.partial for the arguments that do not come from the payload. The context is passed after the bound arguments:

>>> import functools
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def save(path: str, context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"save epoch {context['epoch']} to {path}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", functools.partial(save, "model.pt"))
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 4})
save epoch 4 to model.pt

docs.title: Run a handler once
docs.text:
once=True removes the registration just before its handler runs. With a condition, it waits for the first trigger where the condition is True:

>>> from minevent import AfterNCondition, EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> subscription = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end", lambda: print("saved"), once=True, condition=AfterNCondition(2)
... )
>>> for _ in range(4):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end")
saved
>>> subscription.active
False

docs.title: Remove a handler
docs.text:
Keep the Subscription returned by add_event_handler to remove exactly that registration. A with block removes it when the block exits, which suits a handler that lives for one phase of the program:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> with manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", lambda: print("profiling")):
...     manager.trigger_event("batch_end")
profiling
>>> manager.trigger_event("batch_end")
>>> len(manager)
0

manager.clear_event("batch_end") removes all the handlers of an event, and manager.reset() removes all the handlers of all the events.

docs.title: Write a plugin
docs.text:
A plugin registers its handlers when it is set up, and keeps the subscriptions to remove them when it is torn down:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> class ProgressPlugin:
...     def setup(self, manager: EventManager) -> None:
...         self.subscriptions = [
...             manager.add_event_handler("epoch_start", self.on_epoch_start),
...             manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", self.on_epoch_end),
...         ]
...
...     def teardown(self) -> None:
...         for subscription in self.subscriptions:
...             subscription.remove()
...
...     def on_epoch_start(self, context: Context) -> None:
...         print(f"start {context['epoch']}")
...
...     def on_epoch_end(self, context: Context) -> None:
...         print(f"end {context['epoch']}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> plugin = ProgressPlugin()
>>> plugin.setup(manager)
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_start", {"epoch": 0})
start 0
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 0})
end 0
>>> plugin.teardown()
>>> len(manager)
0

docs.title: Use coroutine handlers
docs.text:
atrigger_event awaits the coroutine handlers and also runs the synchronous ones, one after the other, in the registration order. trigger_event raises a TypeError for a coroutine handler:

>>> import asyncio
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> async def notify(context: Context) -> None:
...     await asyncio.sleep(0)
...     print(f"notified epoch {context['epoch']}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda context: print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}"))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", notify)
>>> asyncio.run(manager.atrigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1}))
epoch 1
notified epoch 1

docs.title: Trigger events from an async function
docs.text:
In an async program, await the trigger inside your coroutines. The handlers of an event still run one after the other, so the next step starts when every handler is done:

>>> import asyncio
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> async def fetch_all(manager: EventManager, urls: list[str]) -> None:
...     await manager.atrigger_event("fetch_start", {"count": len(urls)})
...     for url in urls:
...         await asyncio.sleep(0)  # a real program awaits a request here
...         await manager.atrigger_event("fetch_done", {"url": url})
...     await manager.atrigger_event("fetch_end")
>>> async def log_done(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"fetched {context['url']}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "fetch_start", lambda context: print(f"fetching {context['count']} urls")
... )
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("fetch_done", log_done)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("fetch_end", lambda: print("done"))
>>> asyncio.run(fetch_all(manager, ["a.com", "b.com"]))
fetching 2 urls
fetched a.com
fetched b.com
done

docs.title: Use options with coroutine handlers
docs.text:
once, condition and the on decorator work the same way with coroutine handlers:

>>> import asyncio
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> @manager.on("epoch_end", condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=2))
... async def upload(context: Context) -> None:
...     await asyncio.sleep(0)
...     print(f"uploaded epoch {context['epoch']}")
>>> async def main() -> None:
...     for epoch in range(3):
...         await manager.atrigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch, "loss": 0.5})
>>> asyncio.run(main())
uploaded epoch 0
uploaded epoch 2

docs.title: Run the work of a handler concurrently
docs.text:
The handlers of an event run sequentially, so a slow handler delays the next ones. To run several awaitables at the same time, use asyncio.gather inside one handler:

>>> import asyncio
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> async def upload(name: str) -> str:
...     await asyncio.sleep(0)
...     return name
>>> async def upload_all(context: Context) -> None:
...     done = await asyncio.gather(*(upload(name) for name in context["files"]))
...     print(f"uploaded {done}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("training_end", upload_all)
>>> asyncio.run(manager.atrigger_event("training_end", {"files": ["a.pt", "b.pt"]}))
uploaded ['a.pt', 'b.pt']

A synchronous handler blocks the event loop while it runs: hand a long computation to an executor (await loop.run_in_executor(...) or asyncio.to_thread) from a coroutine handler.

docs.title: Handle an async handler used with trigger_event
docs.text:
trigger_event is synchronous, so it cannot await a coroutine. It closes the coroutine and raises a TypeError that names the handler, instead of silently dropping it:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> async def notify() -> None:
...     print("notified")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", notify)
>>> try:
...     manager.trigger_event("my_event")
... except TypeError as exc:
...     print(exc)
notify returned an awaitable; use atrigger_event

docs.title: Handle the errors of a handler
docs.text:
A handler that raises stops the dispatch, and the exception reaches the caller with a note that names the event and the handler:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def fail() -> None:
...     raise ValueError("boom")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", fail)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", lambda: print("not reached"))
>>> try:
...     manager.trigger_event("my_event")
... except ValueError as exc:
...     print(exc, "|", exc.__notes__[0])
boom | raised by fail while handling the event 'my_event'

To keep the other handlers running, catch the exception in the handler.

docs.title: Test a handler
docs.text:
A handler is a plain callable, so test it without a manager. Test the wiring with a mock:

from unittest.mock import Mock

from minevent import EventManager


def test_epoch_end_calls_the_handler():
    manager = EventManager()
    handler = Mock()
    manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", handler)
    manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1})
    handler.assert_called_once_with({"epoch": 1})

An async handler is tested with asyncio.run (or the async support of your test framework):

import asyncio
from unittest.mock import AsyncMock

from minevent import EventManager


def test_epoch_end_awaits_the_handler():
    manager = EventManager()
    handler = AsyncMock()
    manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", handler)
    asyncio.run(manager.atrigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1}))
    handler.assert_awaited_once_with({"epoch": 1})

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
docs.text: The answers are short; the user guide has the details and the quickstart the runnable examples.

docs.title: What is minevent?
docs.text: minevent is a minimal event system for Python, designed for Machine Learning workflows. You register event handlers, and they run when an event is triggered, so you can add logging, monitoring or checkpointing to a training loop without changing it.

docs.title: How is minevent different from other event systems?
docs.text: It is minimal: events are strings, trigger_event is synchronous (atrigger_event awaits coroutine handlers), handlers run in the registration order, and it has no dependency.

docs.title: What Python versions are supported?
docs.text: Python 3.11 and above. Install it with pip install minevent; see Get Started.

docs.title: Can I use it with PyTorch, TensorFlow or scikit-learn?
docs.text: Yes. minevent does not depend on any ML framework.

docs.title: How do I pass data to the handlers?
docs.text: As a dict, the second argument of trigger_event: manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 3}), or as a Context, which is reused as is: manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", Context({"epoch": 3})). See the payload. Use functools.partial for the arguments that are fixed at registration.

docs.title: How do I run a handler only sometimes?
docs.text: Give the registration a condition, for example condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=5), or any function that returns a boolean. See conditions.

docs.title: How do I run a handler only once?
docs.text: manager.add_event_handler("my_event", handler, once=True).

docs.title: How do I remove a handler?
docs.text: Call remove() on the Subscription returned by add_event_handler. See subscriptions.

docs.title: How do I know if a handler is registered?
docs.text: subscription.active, or look at manager.get_subscriptions("my_event"). Event handlers are compared by identity.

docs.title: What happens if I trigger an event with no handler?
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: In which order do the handlers run?
docs.text: In the order they were registered. A handler added by a running handler runs at the next trigger. A registration removed by a running handler before its turn does not run.

docs.title: What happens if a handler raises?
docs.text: The exception propagates to the caller of trigger_event, with a note that names the event and the handler, and the next handlers are skipped.

docs.title: Can I use coroutine handlers?
docs.text: Yes, with await manager.atrigger_event(...). trigger_event raises a TypeError for a coroutine handler.

docs.title: Is it thread-safe?
docs.text: The registry is: you can register handlers in one thread and trigger events from others. The handlers run in the triggering thread, concurrently if several threads trigger the same event, and the counter of a stateful condition is not protected. See Thread Safety.

docs.title: Can I create custom handlers and conditions?
docs.text: Yes. A handler is any callable: write a class with a __call__(self, context) method (or async def __call__ for atrigger_event). A condition is any function that returns a boolean (it can take the Context of the trigger), or a class with __call__.

docs.title: What is the overhead?
docs.text: About 0.33 µs per trigger with one trivial handler and no data (0.7 µs with a small dict). See performance.

docs.title: Where can I report a bug or ask for a feature?
docs.text: On the GitHub issue tracker.

docs.title: How can I contribute?
docs.text: See the contributing guide.

docs.title: Get Started
docs.text: It is highly recommended to install in a virtual environment to keep your system in order.

docs.title: Installing with pip (recommended)
docs.text:
We highly recommend installing a virtual environment. minevent can be installed from pip using the following command:

pip install minevent

minevent has no dependency, so no optional dependencies or extras are required.

docs.title: Installing from source
docs.text: To install minevent from source, you can follow the steps below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This project uses uv for dependency management. If you don't have uv installed, you can install it by following the official installation guide.

docs.title: Clone the repository
docs.text:
First, clone the git repository:

git clone git@github.com:durandtibo/minevent.git
cd minevent

docs.title: Create a virtual environment (optional but recommended)
docs.text:
It is recommended to create a Python 3.11+ virtual environment. You can use uv to create a virtual environment:

uv venv --python 3.13
source .venv/bin/activate

docs.title: Install dependencies
docs.text:
Once you have activated your virtual environment, install the required packages with:

inv env.install

Or if you're developing and need documentation dependencies:

inv env.install --docs-deps

These commands will install all the required packages. You can also use these commands to update the required packages.

Finally, you can test the installation by running the test suite:

docs.title: User guide
docs.text: This guide collects the recommendations, the patterns and the troubleshooting tips for using minevent. The quickstart explains the API step by step, and the architecture page lists the guarantees of the library.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
An event is a case-sensitive str. Any other type raises a TypeError.

  • Name the event after what happened, in the past tense: epoch_end, checkpoint_saved, not event1 or done.
  • Pick one convention for the whole project, for example snake_case (batch_end) or a namespace (training.batch.end). Names are only strings, so minevent has no notion of hierarchy.
  • Define the names in one place (constants or an Enum with str values) to avoid typos: the events "epoch_end" and "epoch-end" are different, and triggering an event without handler does nothing.

docs.title: Keep handlers focused
docs.text: One handler does one thing (log, save, update a progress bar). Handlers of an event run in the order they were registered, so register them in the order they must run.

docs.title: Pass the data as a payload
docs.text:
The second argument of trigger_event is a mapping from str to values (a dict, for example). It is copied into a read-only Context, which is built once per trigger and passed to every handler that has a parameter. A Context is also accepted, and is passed as is (it is immutable, so it can be reused for several triggers); None, or no argument, means no data:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def log_epoch(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}: {context['loss']}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", log_epoch)
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 3, "loss": 0.5})
epoch 3: 0.5

Both forms are equivalent for the handlers: manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 3}) and manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", Context({"epoch": 3})). Pass a dict for a one-off trigger, and build a Context once to reuse it for several triggers (it is validated and copied only once).

A Context is a read-only mapping from str to values: a handler cannot change what the next handler sees (the values are not copied, so a mutable value stays mutable). Each handler reads the keys it needs and decides what to do when one is missing, so handlers with different needs share an event and an extra key never breaks a handler:

  • context["loss"] reads a required value and raises a KeyError that lists the available keys.
  • context.get("loss", 0.0) reads an optional value.
  • "loss" in context, len(context), context.items() and dict(context) work as for a mapping.
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def log_epoch(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}, loss {context.get('loss', 'unknown')}")
>>> def say_hello() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", log_epoch)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", say_hello)
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 3})
epoch 3, loss unknown
Hello!

A handler that has a parameter that accepts a positional argument (or a *args) is called as handler(context), and a handler without parameter is called as handler(). This is decided once, when the handler is registered, from the number of parameters: the names are never matched. A callable whose signature cannot be inspected is called as handler(context).

Bind the arguments that do not come from the payload with functools.partial: the context is passed after the bound positional arguments.

docs.title: Handle the exceptions
docs.text:
Handlers run fail-fast: if a handler raises, the exception reaches the caller of trigger_event and the next handlers of the event do not run. The exception is the original one, with a note that names the event and the function of the handler (never its arguments):

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def fail() -> None:
...     raise ValueError("boom")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", fail)
>>> try:
...     manager.trigger_event("my_event")
... except ValueError as exc:
...     print(exc.__notes__[0])
raised by fail while handling the event 'my_event'

If the failure of a handler must not stop the training, catch the exception in the handler. There is no option to collect the errors of all the handlers (see the non-goals in the architecture page).

docs.title: Async handlers
docs.text: trigger_event is synchronous. A handler that returns an awaitable (a coroutine function) raises a TypeError there, instead of silently dropping the coroutine. Use atrigger_event to await the handlers, one after the other, in the registration order. Synchronous handlers can be mixed with coroutine handlers, and they block the event loop while they run.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
A condition is a function that returns a boolean. It is called each time the event is triggered, before the handler, and the handler runs only if it returns True. A condition that has a parameter is called with the read-only Context of the trigger, like a handler (see Pass the data as a payload), and a condition without parameter is called without argument:

from minevent import PeriodicCondition

# Save a checkpoint every 10 epochs, and log every 100 batches
manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", save_checkpoint, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=10))
manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", log_batch, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=100))

# Any function works as a condition
manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", notify, condition=lambda: is_main_process)

# A condition with a parameter reads the payload of the trigger
manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", validate, condition=lambda context: context["epoch"] >= 5)
  • PeriodicCondition and AfterNCondition keep a counter. Do not share one instance between two handlers: they would advance the same counter. Create one per handler. Call reset() to restart the counter.
  • To combine conditions, write a function. lambda: a() and b() skips b when a is False; lambda: all([a(), b()]) evaluates both, so stateful conditions advance together.
  • A stateful condition is not protected by a lock: call it from one thread.

docs.title: Create it in one place
docs.text:
Create the manager once and pass it where it is needed. minevent has no global manager on purpose: it keeps the tests independent and makes the ownership clear.

def main():
    manager = EventManager()
    setup_handlers(manager)
    Trainer(manager).train()


def setup_handlers(manager: EventManager) -> None:
    manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", save_checkpoint)
    manager.add_event_handler("training_end", log_summary)

A manager is always truthy, even when it is empty, so manager or EventManager() keeps the manager you pass; use len(manager) for the number of registrations. A manager cannot be copied or pickled (copy.copy, copy.deepcopy and pickle raise a TypeError): create a new one.

docs.title: Register any callable
docs.text:
add_event_handler accepts any callable, called as handler(context) or handler() (see Pass the data as a payload): a function, a method, a callable object or a functools.partial. The options of the registration are its keyword-only arguments: once and condition. Use functools.partial to bind the arguments that do not come from the payload.

>>> import functools
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> def greet(name: str) -> None:
...     print(f"Hello {name}!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", functools.partial(greet, "Bob"))
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello Bob!
>>> def log_epoch(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}")
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end", log_epoch, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=2)
... )
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1, "loss": 0.5})
epoch 1
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 2, "loss": 0.4})

The signature of a functools.partial does not contain the arguments that it binds: a partial that binds the only positional parameter of a function is called as handler().

docs.title: Keep the subscription
docs.text:
add_event_handler returns a Subscription, the registration of the handler. It is the only way to identify a registration: the same callable can be registered several times, and each registration is a different Subscription.

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> subscription = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", print)
>>> subscription.active
True
>>> subscription.remove()
True
>>> subscription.remove()
False
  • remove() removes that registration only, once. It returns False if the registration is already gone (removed, or cleared by clear_event or reset, or consumed by once=True).
  • with manager.add_event_handler(...): removes the registration when the block exits, which is convenient for a profiler or a progress bar that lives for one phase of the program.
  • manager.get_subscriptions(event) lists the registrations of an event if you did not keep them, and subscription.handler gives the handler.
  • @manager.on("event") registers a function as a handler and returns it unchanged. It takes once and condition, as in @manager.on("epoch_end", once=True), which are also the keyword-only arguments of add_event_handler. Use add_event_handler if you need the Subscription.
  • once=True runs the handler the first time its condition is True (at the next trigger if it has no condition), then removes the registration. A condition that is False does not consume it.

docs.title: Avoid duplicates
docs.text:
Registering the same handler twice runs it twice. To register it once, look at the registrations:

if not any(sub.handler is handler for sub in manager.get_subscriptions("my_event")):
    manager.add_event_handler("my_event", handler)

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
A registered handler lives as long as the manager: obj.method keeps obj alive, and so do the arguments bound by a functools.partial and closures. minevent uses no weak reference. Remove the subscriptions of the objects you no longer need, use a with block, or call clear_event / reset:

try:
    trainer.train(manager)
finally:
    manager.reset()

docs.title: Training loop
docs.text:
class Trainer:
    def __init__(self, model, manager: EventManager) -> None:
        self.model = model
        self.manager = manager

    def train(self, epochs: int, loader) -> None:
        self.manager.trigger_event("training_start")
        for epoch in range(epochs):
            self.manager.trigger_event("epoch_start", {"epoch": epoch})
            for batch in loader:
                loss = self.step(batch)
                self.manager.trigger_event("batch_end", {"epoch": epoch, "loss": loss})
            self.manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch})
        self.manager.trigger_event("training_end")

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
A plugin registers its own handlers, and keeps the subscriptions to unregister them:

class LoggingPlugin:
    def setup(self, manager: EventManager) -> None:
        self.subscription = manager.add_event_handler("training_end", self.log_training_complete)

    def teardown(self) -> None:
        self.subscription.remove()

    def log_training_complete(self) -> None:
        print("Training completed!")

docs.title: Custom handlers and conditions
docs.text: Write a class with a __call__(self, context) method for a handler with its own state (use async def __call__ for a coroutine). A condition is any class with a __call__(self) -> bool method.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Test a handler without a manager, and the wiring with a mock:

from unittest.mock import Mock


def test_epoch_end_calls_handler():
    manager = EventManager()
    mock = Mock()
    manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", mock)
    manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1})
    mock.assert_called_once_with({"epoch": 1})


def test_handler_directly():
    handler = functools.partial(print, "test")
    handler()

Use a new EventManager in each test, and manager.reset() if the manager is shared.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
import minevent is cheap: it imports the standard library modules threading, functools, collections.abc and typing only, and not logging, inspect, asyncio or importlib.metadata (inspect is imported when the first handler is registered, and importlib.metadata when __version__ is read). It creates no typing object (Protocol, NamedTuple, TypeVar). It takes a few milliseconds, so a script can import it without a measurable cost.

The cost of trigger_event is the cost of the handlers: about 0.33 µs for a manager with one trivial handler and no data, 0.7 µs with a small dict (it is copied into a Context), and about 0.1 µs for each additional handler on a laptop. A condition avoids the work of an expensive handler (PeriodicCondition). To find a slow handler, time it or wrap it (see Debug).

A handler that is slow blocks the caller. Hand the work to an executor in the handler if the caller must not wait.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• A handler that retriggers its own event recurses until RecursionError. Use a different event or a flag.
  • A handler added during a trigger runs at the next trigger. The registrations that exist when the trigger starts are visited. A registration removed before its turn does not run, whatever removes it (remove(), clear_event, reset). A remove() from another thread cannot stop a handler that the trigger is about to call.
  • The payload is shared: all handlers get the same Context, which is read-only, and the same value objects. A handler that mutates a mutable value (a list, for example) is seen by the next handlers.
  • Threads: the registry is thread-safe, the handlers run in the thread that triggers the event, concurrently if several threads trigger it. A handler that shares state must protect it.

docs.title: My handler does not run
docs.text:
1. The handler is registered for that event: manager.get_subscriptions("my_event").
  2. The event name matches exactly (case-sensitive).
  3. The condition returns True (a PeriodicCondition(freq=5) skips four calls out of five).
  4. It was not registered with once=True and already consumed: subscription.active is False.
  5. A handler of the same event ahead of it raised: the next handlers are skipped.

docs.title: KeyError: "key 'epoch' not found in the context; ..."
docs.text: The trigger did not give the key that the handler requires. The message lists the available keys. Read an optional value with context.get("epoch", default), or check "epoch" in context.

docs.title: TypeError: ... takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given
docs.text: The handler has no parameter that accepts the context, but its signature cannot be inspected, so it is called as handler(context). Wrap it in a function without parameter, or in a function that takes the context.

docs.title: TypeError: ... returned an awaitable; use atrigger_event
docs.text: The handler is a coroutine function (a coroutine object is closed, so Python does not warn that it was never awaited). Call await manager.atrigger_event(...).

docs.title: subscription.remove() returns False
docs.text: The registration is already removed. This is not an error: remove() is idempotent.

docs.title: Debug
docs.text:
• print(manager) shows the number of handlers of each event, and manager.get_subscriptions(e) the registrations; each one prints its event and the name of its handler (Subscription(event='my_event', handler='print')).
  • minevent does not log. Wrap a handler to trace it (the wrapper is a plain callable):
import functools


def traced(handler):
    @functools.wraps(handler)  # the signature of the handler decides if it gets the context
    def wrapper(*args):
        print(f"calling {handler.__qualname__}")
        return handler(*args)

    return wrapper


manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", traced(log_batch))
  • Register a handler that prints the payload while you investigate:
manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", lambda context: print(dict(context)))

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The minevent event system is composed of three main components:

  • an event
  • an event handler (any callable)
  • an event manager

trigger_event is synchronous: the handlers of an event run one after the other, in the order they were registered, in the calling thread. Coroutine handlers are supported by atrigger_event (see Fire an event with coroutine handlers). This page presents the design used in minevent, but other designs exist. The proposed design was not designed to work in all the scenarios, so it is highly recommended to read the documentation to understand if it fits your needs and requirements before using it.

docs.title: Event
docs.text:
In minevent, an event is a string that represents something happening. The event is represented by the event name. For example, it is possible to write the following line to define an event that happens after the training is completed.

my_event = "training completed"

docs.title: Event handler
docs.text:
In minevent, an event handler is a piece of code that is executed when an event happens.

An event handler is any callable. It is called as handler(context) if it has a parameter, and as handler() otherwise, where context is a read-only Context that holds the data given when the event is triggered (see Fire an event). A coroutine function is a handler of atrigger_event. The options of a registration (once and condition) are the keyword-only arguments of EventManager.add_event_handler.

docs.title: Basic event handler
docs.text:
Let's assume we want to create an event handler to say hello when an event is fired. A function is a handler:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!

docs.title: Event handler with arguments
docs.text:
The previous example has no arguments. It is also possible to provide some arguments to customize the event handler. Use functools.partial to bind the arguments that do not come from the payload. The arguments can be given as positional arguments:

>>> import functools
>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler(name: str, day: str) -> None:
...     print(f"Hello {name}! Happy {day}!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", functools.partial(hello_handler, "Bob", "Monday"))
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello Bob! Happy Monday!

as keyword arguments:

>>> import functools
>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler(name: str, day: str) -> None:
...     print(f"Hello {name}! Happy {day}!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "my_event", functools.partial(hello_handler, name="Bob", day="Monday")
... )
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello Bob! Happy Monday!

or both:

>>> import functools
>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler(name: str, day: str) -> None:
...     print(f"Hello {name}! Happy {day}!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", functools.partial(hello_handler, "Bob", day="Monday"))
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello Bob! Happy Monday!

It is possible to define event handlers with a large range of functions. For example, it is possible to implement the same logic with a lambda function. Note that a callable that accepts *args, like print, receives the context as an argument, so a handler that does not need the context must not have a parameter:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", lambda: print("Hello Bob! Happy Monday!"))
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello Bob! Happy Monday!

docs.title: Event handler with condition
docs.text:
It is possible to define an event handler that is executed when a condition is true. The following example shows how to define an event handler where the logic is executed every three calls.

>>> from minevent import EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=3))
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!

PeriodicCondition is a condition implemented in minevent to execute an event handler with a periodic pattern. It is also possible to implement custom conditions. If the condition returns True, the logic associated to the event handler is executed, otherwise the logic associated to the event handler is not executed.

A plain function without argument that returns a boolean is also accepted as a condition:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> verbose = True
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler, condition=lambda: verbose)
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!

A condition is any function that returns a boolean (a Condition). Like a handler, it is called as condition() if it has no parameter, and as condition(context) with the read-only Context of the trigger if it has one, so it can depend on the payload:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end",
...     lambda: print("late epoch"),
...     condition=lambda context: context.get("epoch", 0) >= 2,
... )
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1})
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 2})
late epoch

minevent provides the stateful conditions AfterNCondition (skip the first n calls) and PeriodicCondition(freq, skip_first=...). A class with a __call__ method is a condition too.

To combine conditions, write a function. You choose which conditions are evaluated:

>>> from minevent import AfterNCondition, EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> after_one, periodic = AfterNCondition(1), PeriodicCondition(2)
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "my_event", hello_handler, condition=lambda: all([after_one(), periodic()])
... )
>>> for _ in range(5):
...     manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!
Hello!

all([a(), b()]) evaluates every condition at each call, so stateful conditions advance together. a() and b() skips b when a is False: use it when b is costly and stateless, because a stateful b would not count the calls skipped by a.

Stateful conditions (PeriodicCondition, AfterNCondition) keep their counter in the instance. A condition instance given to two handlers is shared, so the two handlers advance the same counter. Create one instance per handler (a small factory function is enough):

>>> import functools
>>> from minevent import EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> def say(name):
...     print(name)
>>> def register(name):
...     manager.add_event_handler(
...         name, functools.partial(say, name), condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=2)
...     )
>>> register("first")
>>> register("second")
>>> manager.trigger_event("first")
first
>>> manager.trigger_event("second")
second

To run a handler once, use add_event_handler(..., once=True): the registration is removed just before its handler runs, on the next trigger of the event whose condition is True.

docs.title: Event handler identity
docs.text:
Registrations are identified by the Subscription that EventManager.add_event_handler returns, not by the handler: the same callable can be registered several times. To find or remove a registration, keep the Subscription (see Subscriptions).

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> first = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", print)
>>> second = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", print)
>>> first == second
False
>>> first.handler is second.handler
True

docs.title: Overview of the event manager
docs.text:
As explained by its name, the goal of the event manager is to manage event handlers. The event manager supports the following functionalities:

  • adding an event handler, which returns a Subscription (add_event_handler, on)
  • firing all the event handlers associated to an event, with an optional payload (trigger_event, atrigger_event)
  • inspecting the registrations (events, get_subscriptions, len(manager))
  • removing an event handler from an event (Subscription.remove, clear_event, reset)

docs.title: Create an event manager
docs.text:
To use the event system, it is important to create an event manager. minevent implements one event manager, EventManager. It has no global state, so you create an instance and pass it where it is needed. To create an event manager, you can write:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> manager
EventManager(events={})

The representation of the event manager shows the number of event handlers of each event. The event manager is empty, so it shows there is no event handler. manager.events lists the events that have at least one handler, and "my_event" in manager tests one.

docs.title: Add an event handler
docs.text:
This section describes how to add an event handler to an event manager. The method to add an event handler to the event manager is add_event_handler. There are several approaches to add an event handler.

The simplest approach requires an event and an event handler. The following example shows how to add a hello_handler handler to the 'my_event' event.

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 1})

You can see there is a registered event handler for the event name my_event.

It is possible to add an event handler that takes some input arguments. The following example shows how to add an event handler with some positional arguments.

>>> import functools
>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler(first_name: str, last_name: str) -> None:
...     print(f"Hello. I am {last_name}, {first_name} {last_name}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", functools.partial(hello_handler, "John", "Smith"))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", functools.partial(hello_handler, "Jane", "Doe"))
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 2})

For a given event, the event handlers run in the order of addition: here, the handler of John Smith runs before the handler of Jane Doe. Internally, each event stores its registrations in an ordered dict. It is possible to add the same event handler multiple times:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 2})

docs.title: Subscriptions
docs.text:
add_event_handler returns a Subscription, the registration of the handler. Its remove() method removes exactly that registration, even if the same handler is registered several times, and returns False if it was already removed:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> handler = hello_handler
>>> first = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", handler)
>>> second = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", handler)
>>> first.remove()
True
>>> first.remove()
False
>>> second.active
True
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!

get_subscriptions returns the registrations of an event, in the order the handlers run, and len(manager) is the total number of registrations. If you want to add an event handler only once, check the registrations:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> handler = hello_handler
>>> for _ in range(5):
...     if not any(s.handler is handler for s in manager.get_subscriptions("my_event")):
...         _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", handler)
>>> len(manager)
1

To run a handler only once, use once=True:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler, once=True)
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")

once=True means "the first time the handler runs": a condition that is False does not consume the registration, which waits for the first trigger where the condition is True:

>>> from minevent import AfterNCondition, EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler, once=True, condition=AfterNCondition(2))
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")

A Subscription is a context manager that removes the registration when the block exits, and its active property tells if the handler is still registered. EventManager.on is a decorator that registers a function and returns it unchanged. It takes the options once and condition:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> with manager.add_event_handler("my_event", lambda: print("Hello!")) as sub:
...     manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!
>>> sub.active
False
>>> @manager.on("epoch_end")
... def log_epoch(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}")
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1})
epoch 1

docs.title: Fire an event
docs.text:
This section describes how to fire an event. As explained above, it is possible to add a handler to an event. Then, we want to execute the handler when the event is fired. The following example shows how to fire the hello_handler for the event 'my_event':

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 1})
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 1})

Triggering an event does not change the manager: the representation above is the same before and after. A handler is called as handler(context), where context holds the data given to trigger_event (see below), or as handler() if it has no parameter. The arguments that do not come from the payload are bound with functools.partial.

>>> import functools
>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler(first_name: str, last_name: str) -> None:
...     print(f"Hello. I am {first_name} {last_name}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", functools.partial(hello_handler, "John", "Smith"))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", functools.partial(hello_handler, "Jane", "Doe"))
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 2})
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello. I am John Smith
Hello. I am Jane Doe

As explained above, it is possible to add a condition to control when to execute the handler. The following shows how to execute the hello_handler every 3 'my_event' events.

>>> from minevent import EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=3))
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 1})
>>> for i in range(10):
...     print(f"i={i}")
...     manager.trigger_event("my_event")
i=0
Hello!
i=1
i=2
i=3
Hello!
i=4
i=5
i=6
Hello!
i=7
i=8
i=9
Hello!

The trigger_event method does nothing if there is no event handler registered for the event:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")

docs.title: Share an event between handlers that need different payload keys
docs.text:
The dict given to trigger_event is copied into one read-only Context that is shared by the handlers. You can also give a Context yourself, trigger_event("epoch_end", Context({...})): it is passed as is, so it can be reused for several triggers. Each handler reads the keys it needs: context["key"] raises a KeyError (that lists the available keys) if the key is missing, and context.get("key", default) returns a default. An extra key never breaks a handler:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def log_loss(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"loss {context['loss']}")
>>> def log_epoch(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}, lr {context.get('lr', 0.1)}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", log_loss)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", log_epoch)
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 3, "loss": 0.5})
loss 0.5
epoch 3, lr 0.1

docs.title: Fire an event with coroutine handlers
docs.text:
trigger_event calls the handlers synchronously and raises a TypeError for a coroutine function (the coroutine would never be awaited). To use coroutine handlers, fire the event with atrigger_event, which awaits the coroutines (and also runs synchronous handlers) one after the other, in the order they were added:

>>> import asyncio
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> async def hello_handler(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"Hello {context['name']}!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> asyncio.run(manager.atrigger_event("my_event", {"name": "John"}))
Hello John!

docs.title: Remove an event handler
docs.text:
A previous section describes how to add an event handler, but sometimes it is useful to remove an event handler. Call remove() on the Subscription returned by add_event_handler:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> subscription = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 1})
>>> subscription.remove()
True
>>> manager
EventManager(events={})

If you did not keep the subscription, get_subscriptions returns the registrations of an event, and clear_event removes all the event handlers of an event:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", print)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_other_event", hello_handler)
>>> manager.get_subscriptions("my_event")[0].remove()
True
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 1, 'my_other_event': 1})
>>> manager.clear_event("my_event")
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_other_event': 1})

docs.title: Reset the event manager
docs.text:
It is possible to reset the event manager with the reset method. It removes all the event handlers and makes their subscriptions inactive. It is equivalent to create a new event manager.

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_other_event", hello_handler)
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 1, 'my_other_event': 1})
>>> manager.reset()
>>> manager
EventManager(events={})

docs.title: minevent
docs.text:
Contain the main features of the minevent package.

minevent is a minimal event system with three concepts: an event (a case-sensitive string), a handler (any callable) and an event manager (EventManager) that stores the handlers and triggers the events.

  • EventManager.add_event_handler (or the on decorator) registers a handler and returns a Subscription, the registration itself, that removes exactly that registration.
  • EventManager.trigger_event runs the handlers in the order they were registered and passes its context argument (a mapping, the payload) to them in a read-only Context. EventManager.atrigger_event also awaits the coroutine handlers.
  • A condition is any function that returns a boolean, without parameter or with the Context of the trigger (Condition). PeriodicCondition and AfterNCondition are provided, and they control when a handler runs.

The package has no dependency, and __version__ is the version of the installed package.

Example 
>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda context: print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}"))
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 3})
epoch 3

docs.text:
Implement a condition that is False for the first n calls and True afterwards.

The condition is stateful, like PeriodicCondition: each call advances the counter, so do not share one instance between several handlers, and call it from one thread because the counter is not protected by a lock. Use reset to restart the counter.

Name Type Description Default n int

The number of calls to skip. Must be a non-negative integer.

required

Raises:

if n is not an integer.

if n is negative.

Example 
>>> from minevent import AfterNCondition
>>> condition = AfterNCondition(2)
>>> [condition() for _ in range(4)]
[False, False, True, True]

>>> condition(), condition()
(False, True)
>>> condition.reset()
>>> condition()
